name: Omi.ai — Onboarding Mentor Intelligence
description: An AI onboarding SaaS, currently a working MVP, that turns an employee's recorded and narrated work sessions into a per-role knowledge base, so new hires learn the job with an AI mentor that cites its sources.
context: When someone leaves a company, their know-how usually leaves with them: the processes live in their head, not in a document. Omi.ai solves that by recording how the outgoing employee actually works, then turning it into procedures and a knowledge base the new hire can question.

I designed and built the product end to end: the recording and upload flow, the AI pipeline that writes the procedures, the retrieval system behind the chat, the onboarding guide, the analytics and the marketing site.

Current status: a working MVP, ready for first user tests. In this version, the employee records a work session while explaining it out loud, then uploads it: Omi turns it into procedures added to the role's Brain, and into a written PDF document. This approach was chosen over capturing on-screen actions directly with Microsoft Clarity's open-source recording technology, for two reasons: it delivered a working product for early tests sooner, and there was a real risk that the AI would struggle to understand what happens on screen without someone explaining it. Automatic capture stays on the roadmap, and the product will evolve with test feedback.

work.title: Process capture
work.text: In the MVP, a process is captured as a recorded work session narrated out loud.
points: The employee records their screen while explaining what they do and why, then uploads the video.
The narration is transcribed and key frames are described by a vision model.
Planned next: a browser extension that captures on-screen actions automatically, based on Microsoft Clarity's open-source recording technology.

work.title: AI-written procedures
work.text: From a capture and a spoken narration, Omi drafts a step-by-step procedure (SOP).
points: Every step cites the narration lines and moments of the recording it comes from.
Coverage score and warnings displayed for review.
Nothing is used by the AI until a human has reviewed and published it.
Each procedure is also produced as a written PDF document, ready to share outside the app.

work.title: A "Brain" per role (RAG)
work.text: Published procedures become a searchable knowledge base for each job.
points: One step = one excerpt, embedded and stored in Supabase with pgvector.
Works with OpenAI or Mistral, and falls back to local BM25 search with no API key.
Each excerpt records the model that encoded it, so two indexes are never mixed.

work.title: Omi Companion, the AI mentor
work.text: A chat that answers new hires only from published procedures.
points: Every answer shows its sources (procedure, step, moment in the recording).
Says "I don't know" below a calibrated relevance threshold and suggests who to contact instead.

work.title: Onboarding guide and Obsidian export
work.text: The knowledge base is turned into ready-to-read onboarding material.
points: A five-module guide per role: the job, its rhythm, procedures in learning order, contacts, edge cases.
Flagged as outdated as soon as a published procedure changes; Markdown export.
A full Obsidian vault export where roles, tools and contacts are linked in a graph.

work.title: Measured quality
work.text: The AI is evaluated, not just demoed.
points: Unit tests on masking, procedure generation, chunking and answers.
Evaluation on a demo Brain: 10/10 on known questions and 6/8 on unseen ones; off-topic questions are refused.
Analytics for each role: coverage score, onboarding velocity and blocking points.

name: Kompute — batch AI jobs on idle gaming GPUs
description: Student team project (entrepreneurship class): a marketplace that runs small teams' batch AI jobs on gaming PCs that would otherwise sit idle.
context: Kompute was built as a group project for an entrepreneurship class. The result is a team effort, not mine alone.

It grew out of a personal project I had put on hold: I had hit a technical wall on security, since running other people’s workloads safely on private computers demands a level of sandboxing and isolation expertise I did not have yet. Rather than ship something unsafe, I paused it, and the class gave the team a chance to rethink the idea as a business: who needs it, what it should cost, and what a credible first version looks like.
Kompute is a student project: there are no customers, no providers and no revenue. The site says so openly.
The school project runs from September to December 2026. I may pick Kompute up again later, once I have the security skills it needs and depending on how the AI compute market evolves.

work.title: The idea
work.text: Small AI teams need GPU power for batch work, while millions of gaming GPUs sit unused most of the day. Kompute connects the two.
points: Teams send non-sensitive, interruptible jobs that fit on a single GPU: embeddings, batch inference (classify, tag, summarise), transcription of public audio and similar runs.
Gamers rent out their idle PC and keep 85% of what each job pays.
Not a fit by design: large multi-GPU training, real-time serving, and any personal or confidential data.

work.title: How it works
work.text: Consumer machines can disappear at any moment, so the system is built around that.
points: Each job is split into small chunks, and every finished chunk is saved as a checkpoint.
The agent on the gaming PC pulls work over HTTPS: nothing ever connects into the player’s home network.
PCs send a heartbeat every 2 seconds; after 10 seconds of silence the job goes back to the queue and resumes on another machine from its last checkpoint.
A few random items are recomputed and compared before delivery, and the team receives one result file, in order.

work.title: What it brings
work.text: A cheaper option for work that can wait a few minutes, and a fair deal for the people providing the hardware.
points: For teams: batch compute without renting or maintaining cloud GPUs, with help packaging their first job.
For gamers: income from an idle PC, chosen availability hours, and games always come first (the job moves elsewhere as soon as a game starts).

work.title: Business model, tested in interviews
work.text: Pricing hypotheses put in front of potential users during interviews, not yet validated by payments.
points: 0.30 to 0.40 € per GPU-hour for teams.
15% platform commission, 85% to the provider.

work.title: What is actually built
work.text: A working proof of concept, with an honest line between what runs and what is illustrative.
points: A live demo runs a real embeddings job on a separate worker that saves checkpoints, can be unplugged mid-job and resumes (on a CPU server, not a gaming GPU).
A quote form that stores requests in a database, answered by hand.
The marketplace dashboard (providers, wallet, payouts) is a mock-up with demo data.
